summary: A status report on the Internet Gateway developed by BBN as of September 1982, including message formats and gateway procedures. It is not an implementation specification. This RFC is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A snapshot of how the first internet routers were doing and how they talked to each other, written down as of one month.

questions: how do routers decide where to send packets
subtitle: Design and operations of Internet routers in the early DARPA Internet.

tldr.problem: The early Internet needed specialized devices to forward packets between different networks, and the DARPA Internet community needed to document how these gateways were built and operated.
tldr.mechanism: This document describes the BBN Internet Gateway, which receives packets, validates them, makes routing decisions based on a dynamic routing table, fragments packets if needed, and forwards them. Gateways exchange routing information using the Gateway-to-Gateway Protocol (GGP) to maintain up-to-date routing knowledge.
tldr.outcome: This was a snapshot of operational gateway technology in 1982. The design was superseded by later routing protocols and gateway architectures, but it documented the first generation of Internet routers. The RFC is marked Historic.

today: This RFC is Historic and describes Internet gateway technology as it existed in September 1982. Modern Internet routers are vastly more complex and use different routing protocols (BGP for interdomain routing, OSPF or IS-IS for intradomain routing) and operate at much higher speeds with greater capacity.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
RFC 823 is a status report on the Internet Gateway developed by Bolt Beranek and Newman (BBN) as of September 1982. It describes the design of the gateway used in the DARPA Internet program, updating earlier documents from 1980 and 1981.

The gateway's primary purpose is to route Internet datagrams to their destination networks. The implementation was written in assembly language for the DEC PDP-11 and LSI-11 processors. The document represents a snapshot of the working system at that time, not a final specification, as gateway technology was still evolving.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a report on how the first real internet routers worked and what machines they ran on.

sections.title: Datagram Forwarding Process
sections.content:
When a gateway receives a message, it performs several steps in sequence:

  • Input processing: The gateway checks the local network header for errors and verifies it contains an Internet datagram.
  • Header validation: The gateway validates the IP header by checking the version number, header length, message length, header checksum, and Time to Live field. It also determines if the datagram is addressed to itself or should be forwarded.
  • Routing decision: The gateway uses its Routing Table to determine which network interface should send the datagram and what destination address to use.
  • Fragmentation: If the next network's maximum message size is smaller than the datagram, it is fragmented according to the Internet Protocol Specification.
  • Header rebuild: The Time to Live field is decremented by one and the IP checksum is recomputed.
  • Output: The datagram is enqueued on an output queue for delivery. Each output queue has a limit to prevent slow networks from consuming all gateway buffers.
sections.plainLanguage: A router checks that a message is valid, figures out where it should go, makes it fit if needed, updates some numbers, and sends it out.

sections.title: Dynamic Routing with the Gateway-to-Gateway Protocol
sections.content:
Gateways maintain a dynamic Routing Table with an entry for each reachable network. The table contains the network number and either the address of the nearest neighbor gateway on the shortest path, or an indication that the gateway is directly connected to the network.

The Gateway-to-Gateway Protocol (GGP) allows gateways to exchange routing information and learn the topology of the internet. Gateways determine connectivity to networks by checking if they can send and receive datagrams on their interfaces. They determine connectivity to neighboring gateways using echo messages: if 3 out of 4 echo messages go unanswered, the neighbor is marked as down; if 2 out of 4 echo replies are received, a down neighbor is marked up.

Gateways use a distance metric based on the number of hops. A gateway is zero hops from its directly connected networks, one hop from networks reachable through another gateway, and so on. Routing updates are sent reliably using sequence-numbered messages and acknowledgments.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers keep track of which other routers they can reach and periodically test if they are still working. They share this knowledge so every router knows the best path to every network.

sections.title: Monitoring and Management
sections.content:
The gateway supports several protocols for operational management:

  • Host Monitoring Protocol (HMP): Collects measurements and status information from gateways. Exceptional conditions are reported as HMP traps, and status messages report the state of the gateway's interfaces, neighbors, and reachable networks.
  • ICMP: The gateway generates ICMP messages including Echo Reply, Destination Unreachable, Redirect, Time Exceeded, and Parameter Problem, as defined in the ICMP specification.
  • Cross-Net Debugging Protocol (XNET): Used to load the gateway and examine and deposit data during development and debugging.

The gateway maintains detailed counters for operational monitoring, including per-interface statistics (datagrams received with errors, forwarded, looped, etc.) and per-neighbor statistics (routing updates sent and received, datagrams forwarded, buffers dropped, etc.).
sections.plainLanguage: Routers have ways to report problems and let administrators check on their health without special visits.

sections.title: Software Architecture
sections.content:
The gateway software consists of multiple components organized by function:

  • Device Drivers: Handle communication with each network interface.
  • Network Software: Implements the host-to-network protocol for each attached network type.
  • Shared Gateway Software: Implements the datagram forwarding process, routing algorithm, and management protocols.

The gateway runs several processes including Network Processes for each interface, a GGP Process for routing updates, and an HMP Process for monitoring. The entire system was written in macro-11 assembly language to achieve the space efficiency needed for operation on limited hardware, and to provide the performance required for reliable packet forwarding across multiple networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The router software is organized into pieces: drivers for each network connection, shared code for forwarding packets, and separate processes for routing and monitoring.
